introduction: Today a new Church year begins, and with it the season of Advent. Isaiah cries out to God to tear open the heavens and come down, and Jesus tells his disciples to stay awake, for they do not know when the master of the house will return. Advent is a season of longing and watchfulness. As we light the first candle, let us ask the Lord to wake us from spiritual sleep and to make us ready for his coming.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Our God is faithful, and he comes to save us. With watchful hearts, let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church at the start of this new liturgical year: that she may help all her children to watch and pray as they wait for the Lord. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who govern the nations: that they may work for justice and peace, so that every people may live in security. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who feel that God is far away or silent: that they may come to know him as their Father and Redeemer. Let us pray to the Lord.
For families preparing for Christmas: that amid shopping and celebrations they may make room in their homes for prayer. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our parish community: that this Advent may be a time of conversion, especially through the Sacrament of Reconciliation. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you are our Father; we are the clay and you are the potter. Shape us by your grace in this holy season, and keep us awake for the coming of your Son. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Tear open the heavens
reflection.body:
Advent opens with a cry. The prophet looks at a people who have wandered from God and feel abandoned by him, and he prays with startling boldness: "Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down." It is the prayer of anyone who has waited a long time for God to act.

Isaiah does not pretend that the people are innocent. "we have all become like one who is unclean," he admits. Yet the same passage ends with the most tender image in the prophets: "But now, LORD, you are our Father. We are the clay and you our potter. We all are the work of your hand." The way out of sin is not to hide from God but to place ourselves back in his hands, like clay on the potter's wheel.

Christians know that this prayer was answered. God did tear open the heavens. He came down, not in thunder that makes the mountains quake, but as a child in Bethlehem. Advent prepares us to celebrate that first coming at Christmas.

But the Gospel today looks further ahead, to Christ's coming at the end of time. Jesus tells a short parable of servants left in charge while their master is away. The doorkeeper must stay awake, because the master may return at evening, at midnight, at cockcrow or in the morning. "What I tell you, I tell all: Watch!"

Watching does not mean anxiety or idle waiting. Paul tells the Corinthians that they lack no spiritual gift while they wait for the revelation of the Lord, and that God "will also confirm you until the end." To watch is to live each day as if it matters, because it does: praying, serving, keeping our lamps trimmed.

This Advent, let us choose one simple practice: a few minutes of daily prayer, a good confession, an act of reconciliation. Let us become clay again in the Father's hands, so that when Christ comes, at Christmas and at the end of time, he finds us awake.
